analysis.one_liner: Bans drugmakers from cutting off Canadian pharmacies to keep cheaper prescriptions from reaching Americans.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 69 cosponsors from both parties but never got a committee vote, and the 108th Congress ended with it still sitting in a subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies charge much higher prices in the United States than in Canada, and they have responded to Americans buying drugs from Canadian pharmacies by cutting off or limiting the supply those pharmacies can sell to U.S. customers. This bill would make that practice illegal: no manufacturer could impose contract terms, supply limits, or other measures that leave U.S. consumers worse off than foreign buyers of the same drugs, with civil penalties up to $1 million for violations. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in February 2003 and was sent to its Health Subcommittee, where it stayed without a hearing or vote until Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who buy prescription drugs, especially seniors and others who pay U.S. retail prices that run far above Canadian prices. The bill's findings state that many Americans skip doses or sacrifice other necessities to afford medications, and that roughly two million parcels of prescription drugs for personal use already enter the country from Canada each year. Keeping Canadian supply open would preserve a cheaper alternative for them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans paying U.S. prescription drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill orders the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write rules prohibiting manufacturers from discriminating against U.S. consumers buying prescription medications from Canadian pharmacies [S2].

It defines discrimination to include any contract provision, supply limit, or other measure that gives U.S. consumers worse terms than foreign purchasers, or that otherwise restricts their access to drugs from Canadian pharmacies [S3].
Manufacturers who knowingly violate the ban face a civil penalty of up to $1,000,000 [S3].

The bill's findings state that drug manufacturers charge substantially more in the United States than in Canada, and that many Americans go without needed medications or sacrifice other necessities to afford them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name prescription drug manufacturers, whose higher U.S. prices and supply restrictions on Canadian pharmacies are the direct target of the bill. If the cross-border channel stayed open at scale, those companies would face pressure to narrow the U.S.-Canada price gap, which would cost them revenue on U.S. sales.

drawbacks.text: Safety oversight is the standard objection to drug importation: the FDA cannot independently verify every drug sourced from foreign pharmacies the way it can drugs from the U.S. supply chain, so an open cross-border channel raises a real (though contested) risk of counterfeit or mishandled medicines reaching patients. The bill's supporters answer this by pointing to Canada's comparable approval system, as the bill's own findings note that the Congressional Research Service confirmed the Canadian system is comparable to the U.S. one [S3].

The bill regulates only the Canadian channel. If it worked, manufacturers could respond by narrowing the price gap in other ways, such as reducing the differential that makes Canadian purchases attractive, which would shrink the savings Americans actually see. The bill also leaves U.S. drug prices themselves untouched; it protects an escape valve rather than fixing the underlying pricing system [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who already buy from Canadian pharmacies or cannot afford U.S. prices, the bill offers concrete, immediate help at no cost to them, since it simply forbids manufacturers from blocking the channel; the safety argument is strongest for a broader open-import regime and weakest for the regulated Canada-only flow the bill protects, given Canada's comparable regulatory system. The real limitation is design: it does not address why U.S. prices are so much higher, and manufacturers could erode the savings by repricing. But as a consumer protection measure, the benefits plainly outweigh the drawbacks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee in February 2003, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 13, 2003 by Rep. Bernard Sanders with 33 original cosponsors [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on February 13, 2003 [S5].
On February 26, 2003 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where its action history ends [S5].
The bill gathered 69 cosponsors, 64 Democrats and 5 Republicans, but no committee or subcommittee vote was ever recorded, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the bill died without a vote, so they kept their ability to restrict supply to Canadian pharmacies and to maintain the large gap between U.S. and Canadian prices.

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 33 original cosponsors [S3].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the referred bill for the remainder of the Congress without a markup or vote; action history shows no further committee action after the Health Subcommittee referral [S5].

against.name: Brand-name prescription drug manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The bill's target: manufacturers that restrict supply to or impose contract terms on Canadian pharmacies to prevent U.S. consumers from buying at Canadian prices. The pharmaceutical industry opposed broad importation legislation during this period.

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; no markup or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill sat in the Health Subcommittee until the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but lopsided: 64 of the 69 cosponsors were Democrats and 5 were Republicans, and the Republican chairman of the committee of referral never brought it to a vote.

industries.note: The bill outlaws their practice of restricting supply to or imposing contract terms on Canadian pharmacies, which exists to keep the large U.S.-Canada price gap intact. Their higher U.S. prices are paid directly by American patients, so their financial interest in blocking the bill runs against consumers' access to cheaper medication.

industries.industry: Canadian pharmacies and cross-border drug retailers
industries.note: A legal protection against manufacturers cutting off their supply secures their customer base of U.S. buyers, whose interest in affordable drugs is the same as the pharmacies' interest in selling to them.

They lose some customers to Canadian channels if reimportation grows, but they also benefit from the same cross-border pressure that limits what manufacturers can charge them. The bill does not directly regulate them.
